claims.text: The coating's creep resistance is primarily governed by coherent, chemically distinct FCC/BCC phase boundaries impeding stress-assisted dislocation climb.
FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers that retard plastic deformation during continuous loading.
The initial coating has a continuous FCC matrix containing discrete BCC precipitates with coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
Under sustained loading, deformation in the coating tends to proceed by stress-assisted dislocation climb.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces hinder dislocation climb and thereby limit plastic flow.
A material with effective FCC/BCC phase boundaries has a lower creep rate than a material without such boundaries.
Testing below approximately 0.7 T_m avoids significant dynamic recrystallization or phase transformation.
Under sustained creep testing, the coating should accumulate less creep strain than the unstrained, negligibly loaded time-zero baseline.
Coatings with well-maintained interphase boundaries should show less accelerated dislocation climb than coatings with compromised boundaries.
Coatings with well-maintained interphase boundaries should show less tertiary creep than coatings with compromised boundaries.
The proposed mechanism applies only while dynamic recrystallization, phase transformation, BCC dissolution, and microstructural coarsening do not significantly degrade interface integrity.
Long-term thermal exposure or aging may diminish the interface barrier effect.
Dynamic precipitation or recrystallization may concurrently influence creep behavior.
An appropriate preliminary thermal cycle can selectively disrupt interface order sufficiently to create a compromised-interface comparison group.

If intact-interface coatings do not have both a significantly lower creep strain rate and reduced climb activity relative to disrupted-interface coatings, interface-controlled climb resistance is not the primary creep mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field permits semi-coherent interfaces, whereas the governing hypothesis specifically attributes resistance to coherent interfaces.

The predicted outcome compares a loaded specimen with an unstrained, negligibly loaded time-zero baseline, which cannot reveal reduced creep accumulation. The mechanism and falsification experiment instead require a loaded comparator lacking effective or intact interfaces.
